credit-card-rewards.summary: Credit card reward value depends on eligible spending, earn rates, caps, redemption assumptions and fees. This worksheet separates recurring annual net value from a first-year bonus and compares two manual plans using the same spending budget.
credit-card-rewards.scope: Manual eligible-spending assumptions only. No issuer catalogue, live offer, automatic point valuation, approval or tax determination. Results are before unentered interest and other costs; all spending caps here are annual.

examples.title: Annual cash back cap 0
examples.inputs: spend period = Annual; categories = 12000, 3, 0 / 18000, 1.5, 0; fallback = 1.5; annual fee = 95; usable credits = 0; bonus = 200
steps: Recurring net = annual gross reward value + usable net credits − annual fee; points value = points × cents per point / 100.
With these inputs, gross modeled annual reward value = $630.00.

examples.title: Points at cents value 1
examples.inputs: spend period = Annual; categories = 30000, 2, 0; fallback = 1; cents per point = 1.0; annual fee = 95; usable credits = 0; bonus = 20000
steps: Recurring net = annual gross reward value + usable net credits − annual fee; points value = points × cents per point / 100.
With these inputs, annual points / miles earned = $60,000.00.

examples.title: Flat plan rate A 2
examples.inputs: spend = 30000; rate a = 2; fee a = 95; credits a = 0; rate b = 1; fee b = 0; credits b = 0
steps: Recurring net = annual gross reward value + usable net credits − annual fee; points value = points × cents per point / 100.
With these inputs, recurring annual net advantage (a minus b) = $205.00.
examples.answer: Recurring annual net advantage (A minus B): $205.00.

expected.label: Recurring annual net advantage (A minus B)

questions.question: Are points worth one dollar each?
questions.answer: No. The input is cents per point. At 1 cent each, 60,000 points have an assumed value of $600. Actual redemption terms can differ.

questions.question: Are category caps monthly or annual here?
questions.answer: Annual spend caps only. Monthly spending is annualized, but monthly and quarterly cap resets are not simulated.

questions.question: Does the calculator recommend a bank card?
questions.answer: No. It evaluates your manually entered reward rules and fees without a bank catalogue, live offer or approval check.

questions.question: Does the first-year bonus repeat in annual results?
questions.answer: No. The recurring result excludes the bonus. The first-year result adds only the one-time amount you assumed is earned.

sources.title: Chase: Guide to credit card rewards programs

accounts-receivable-turnover.summary: Receivables turnover compares period net credit sales with representative average trade receivables. Using the same definitions, average-balance DSO converts that turnover into collection days. Reporting-period days and the balance method are part of the result.
accounts-receivable-turnover.scope: Matched-period net credit sales and trade receivables only. The two-point average may miss seasonality. DSO uses average balances here; no closing-balance, countback, aging, bad-debt or customer-credit analysis is provided.

examples.title: average 365 days
steps: Turnover = net credit sales / average trade AR; average-balance DSO = reporting days × average AR / net credit sales.
With these inputs, receivables turnover in selected period = 12.000000.

examples.title: balances 365 days
examples.inputs: days = 365; credit sales = 300000; begin ar = 20000; end ar = 30000
steps: Turnover = net credit sales / average trade AR; average-balance DSO = reporting days × average AR / net credit sales.
With these inputs, receivables turnover in selected period = 12.000000.

questions.question: Can I use total revenue instead of net credit sales?
questions.answer: Only if it represents the credit sales corresponding to the selected receivables. Cash sales and unrelated revenue should not be silently included.

questions.question: Is the turnover result annualized?
questions.answer: No. It is turnover for the selected reporting period. The DSO calculation uses the day count you enter.

questions.question: Why is my published DSO different?
questions.answer: A company may use closing balances, another receivables population or a countback method. This tool uses a representative average and matching net credit sales.

questions.question: What happens when the denominator is zero?
questions.answer: Turnover and DSO are checked separately. Undefined results are labeled explicitly rather than displayed as infinity or a real zero multiple.

days-payable-outstanding.summary: Days payable outstanding converts a matched-period trade-payables balance into an estimated payment period. Purchase-based and COGS-proxy versions can give different answers. This worksheet names the denominator and reports payables turnover alongside the days measure.
days-payable-outstanding.scope: Manual trade payables and matched credit purchases or a named COGS proxy. No inferred credit-purchase share, full inventory roll-forward, supplier aging, contract-term approval or cash-solvency decision.

examples.title: purchases 365 days
steps: Purchase-based DPO = reporting days × average trade AP / net credit purchases; proxy DPO explicitly substitutes COGS.
With these inputs, days payable outstanding = 36.500000.

examples.title: balances 365 days
examples.inputs: days = 365; begin ap = 40000; end ap = 60000; purchases = 500000
steps: Purchase-based DPO = reporting days × average trade AP / net credit purchases; proxy DPO explicitly substitutes COGS.
With these inputs, days payable outstanding = 36.500000.

examples.title: cogs 365 days
steps: Purchase-based DPO = reporting days × average trade AP / net credit purchases; proxy DPO explicitly substitutes COGS.
With these inputs, days payable outstanding = 45.625000.

questions.question: Is COGS exactly the same as credit purchases?
questions.answer: No. Inventory changes, cash purchases and accounting adjustments can make them differ. The COGS mode is an explicit proxy.

questions.question: What goes into average accounts payable?
questions.answer: A representative trade-payables balance for the same purchase or cost period. Beginning/end mode uses the two-point arithmetic mean.

questions.question: Can I calculate a quarter’s DPO?
questions.answer: Yes. Enter that quarter’s purchases or selected cost, average trade payables and actual reporting days.

questions.question: Does a longer DPO mean bills should be delayed?
questions.answer: No. The ratio does not determine supplier terms or whether payments are overdue or appropriate.

cash-conversion-cycle.summary: The cash conversion cycle combines inventory days and collection days, then subtracts payables days. The operating cycle stops before that subtraction. Keeping all three components on compatible definitions allows a meaningful comparison between known-days and financial-input calculations.
cash-conversion-cycle.scope: Manual, matched-period balance ratios or supplied component days. Purchase-based and COGS-proxy payables are separate modes. This is not a cash-balance forecast, liquidity guarantee or supplier-payment instruction.

examples.title: Component days (45, 30, 60)
steps: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO; operating cycle = DIO + DSO.
With these inputs, cash conversion cycle (days) = 15.000000.

examples.title: purchases 365 days
examples.inputs: days = 365; inventory = 80000; cogs = 400000; average ar = 25000; credit sales = 600000; average ap = 50000; purchases = 500000
steps: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO; operating cycle = DIO + DSO.
With these inputs, cash conversion cycle (days) = 51.708333.

examples.title: cogs 365 days
examples.inputs: days = 365; inventory = 80000; cogs = 400000; average ar = 25000; credit sales = 600000; average ap = 50000
steps: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO; operating cycle = DIO + DSO.
With these inputs, cash conversion cycle (days) = 42.583333.

questions.question: Can the cash conversion cycle be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. A negative result can indicate that modeled collections occur before supplier payments. It is retained and explained.

questions.question: Is operating cycle another name for CCC?
questions.answer: No. Operating cycle equals DIO plus DSO. CCC subtracts DPO as well.

questions.question: Why do two calculators give different CCC values?
questions.answer: They may use different balance averages, credit-sales scope, periods or purchase-versus-COGS payables denominators. Compare each component and input definition.

questions.question: Does CCC predict when the business will run out of cash?
questions.answer: No. That requires available cash and cash-flow assumptions. CCC summarizes working-capital timing ratios.

sources.title: OpenStax: Working capital and cash cycles

roic.summary: ROIC compares annual after-tax operating profit with representative average invested capital. It differs from accounting net-income ROE and a general profit-to-cost ROI. The numerator, capital definition, tax assumptions and reporting period must describe the same operating scope.
roic.scope: Annual manual operating-profit and invested-capital assumptions only. No live financial statements, balance-sheet reconstruction, intangible-capital adjustment or stock valuation. Loss tax benefits are not presumed unless explicitly selected.

examples.title: nopat annual operating model
steps: ROIC = annual NOPAT / average invested capital; simplified economic profit = NOPAT − WACC × matching average capital.
With these inputs, annual return on invested capital = 12.00%.

examples.title: ebit annual operating model

values.loss_tax: No assumed tax benefit on a loss

examples.inputs: ebit = 200000; tax rate = 25; loss tax = No assumed tax benefit on a loss; capital = 1250000; wacc = 8
steps: ROIC = annual NOPAT / average invested capital; simplified economic profit = NOPAT − WACC × matching average capital.
With these inputs, annual return on invested capital = 12.00%.

examples.title: balances annual operating model
examples.inputs: nopat = 150000; begin capital = 1000000; end capital = 1500000; wacc = 8
steps: ROIC = annual NOPAT / average invested capital; simplified economic profit = NOPAT − WACC × matching average capital.
With these inputs, annual return on invested capital = 12.00%.

questions.question: Can I use net income instead of NOPAT?
questions.answer: Not silently. NOPAT is operating profit after tax; net income can include financing and non-operating items. Match the earnings and capital scope.

questions.question: Does a loss automatically create a tax benefit here?
questions.answer: No. The default EBIT mode assumes no tax benefit on an operating loss. Applying the simplified tax rate requires an explicit selection.

questions.question: What is the difference between a percent return and a percentage-point spread?
questions.answer: ROIC 12% minus WACC 8% is a 4-percentage-point spread. It is not a 4% relative increase in return.

questions.question: Is invested capital always the market value of debt and equity?
questions.answer: No. Operating/book definitions and adjustments vary. The tool asks for a consistently defined average and does not reconstruct it from market prices.

sources.title: Morgan Stanley: Return on invested capital

interest-coverage-ratio.summary: Interest coverage, also called times interest earned, compares EBIT with same-period interest expense. It measures an earnings-to-interest relationship rather than full principal-and-interest debt service. The selected target is a scenario input, not a universal safe threshold.
interest-coverage-ratio.scope: Manual matched-period EBIT and borrowing-interest expenses, or a simple signed net-income/tax bridge. No EBITDA model, cash-flow forecast, lender approval, default probability or universal covenant threshold.

examples.title: ebit EBIT 100000
steps: ICR / TIE = EBIT / interest expense; required EBIT = selected coverage target × same-period interest expense.
With these inputs, ebit interest coverage (times) = 4.000000.

examples.title: bridge EBIT 100000
examples.inputs: net income = 56000; income tax = 14000; interest = 30000; target = 3
steps: ICR / TIE = EBIT / interest expense; required EBIT = selected coverage target × same-period interest expense.
With these inputs, ebit interest coverage (times) = 3.333333.

questions.question: Is interest coverage the same as DSCR?
questions.answer: No. This ratio uses EBIT and interest expense only. DSCR has its own income definition and debt-service denominator, typically including principal.

questions.question: What if interest expense is zero?
questions.answer: The ratio has no defined denominator. The tool labels it explicitly and does not print infinity or a real zero multiple.

questions.question: Can the coverage ratio be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. Negative EBIT divided by positive interest produces a negative multiple.

questions.question: Is the target multiple a recommended safe minimum?
questions.answer: No. It is a user-selected scenario. The tool does not read covenants, select a lending threshold or predict default.
